items.title: Human-Resource Digital Transformation Trends in Private Universities in India
items.abstract: The digital transformation is reshaping the functioning of academic, administrative and human-resource operations in higher education institutions. The study focuses on the implementation of digital HR in the private Universities of India, specifically on the following digital HR practices: payroll automation, employee self-service, online recruitment, digital performance appraisal, learning management systems, artificial intelligence (AI), and HR analytics. The descriptive survey design was adopted and the data were obtained from 60 HR professionals and administrative personnel in private higher education institutions. The results indicate that high adoption of payroll automation and employee self-service portals and on the other hand, AI-based recruitment and HR analytics are still in their early stages. Financial challenges, employee resistance, lack of digital skills, integration of systems and data-security issues are the main challenges identified. The results have shown that the HR automation process in private Universities is moving from simple automation to more sophisticated and data-oriented HR processes; however, sophisticated digital HR is still at its beginning stage. items.title: Human-Software Trust Over 45 Days of Simulated Spaceflight
items.abstract: Spaceflight operations are a dynamic, safety-critical environment that relies on automated systems. Crew are expected to trust systems throughout the missions. Within the spaceflight context, it remains unclear how trust in software changes over time, and how measures of trust relate to measures of usability. This study presents initial results that longitudinally assess trust in an extreme environment analogous to spaceflight. Over a simulated spaceflight mission, crew interacted with a software tool designed to enhance crew autonomy by allowing them to manage their own schedule. They filled out a software trust questionnaire three times in total, the last time being post-mission. They also filled out a post-mission multidimensional usability questionnaire. Results suggested that trust increased over time, driven by items on security and familiarity. Post-mission trust was positively correlated with usability dimensions of attractiveness, dependability, and efficiency. Software trust emerges as a dynamic phenomenon that is closely linked with usability.

items.title: Humanising assessment in an age of AI
items.abstract: This chapter calls for a humanised approach to assessment in an age of artificial intelligence (AI). It is now more important than ever to ensure that assessment not only captures student learning but also develops students transformatively as future professionals. Students have historically been portrayed as the objects of assessment, yet the surge of AI technologies may be seen as the catalyst needed to move away from assessment that views students as objects moulded by others—as numbers, scores, data points, and targets. This chapter unpacks this hopeful suggestion by discussing how AI technologies could be harnessed for designing ‘humanised’ forms of assessment, providing practical examples of how assessment design could meet this goal. This is an attempt to make use of AI technologies in meaningful ways, without falling into simple techno-solutionism. Without paying attention to these matters, we are at risk of humanising AI technologies—as partners, assistants, chatbots, and helpers—while dehumanising our students. This would run counter to the very purpose of the humanising project of higher education.

items.title: HYBRID NANOTECHNOLOGY FOR HYPERPIGMENTATION: INTEGRATING NANO EMULSION AND METALLIC NANOPARTICLES FOR MULTIFUNCTIONAL MELANIN REGULATION
items.abstract: Hyperpigmentation is a persistent and multifactorial skin disorder characterized by excessive melanin deposition and associated with melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, solar lentigines, freckles, and photoaging. Conventional depigmenting agents and procedures are often limited by poor skin penetration, instability, irritation, recurrence, and inconsistent efficacy. This review evaluates the potential of nanotechnology, focusing on nano emulsions, metallic nanoparticles, and hybrid nano emulsion metallic nanoparticle systems for improved management of hyperpigmentation. The molecular mechanisms of pigmentation are discussed, with emphasis on tyrosinase, microphthalmia-associated transcription factor, tyrosinase-related protein 1, tyrosinase-related protein 2, melanocortin 1 receptor signaling, cyclic adenosine monophosphate signaling, mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, and Wingless-related integration site/β-catenin signaling, together with the roles of oxidative stress, inflammation, melanosome biogenesis, and melanosome transfer. Nano emulsions can enhance solubilization, stability, skin permeation, bioavailability, and controlled release, whereas metallic nanoparticles provide antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, ultraviolet-protective, and melanogenesis-modulating effects. Their integration may improve dispersion, delivery, retention, stability, and targeting while reducing irritation. Future directions include artificial intelligence-assisted formulation, personalized nano therapy, exosome-mediated delivery, stimuli-responsive systems, advanced skin models, green nanotechnology, and clinical translation. However, further research is required to establish long-term safety, optimize particle characteristics, validate efficacy through clinical studies, and facilitate reproducible manufacturing, regulatory approval, and successful commercialization for broader therapeutic and cosmetic applications. Keywords: Hyperpigmentation; Nano emulsion; Metallic nanoparticles; Melanogenesis; Tyrosinase inhibition

items.title: Identification and Prediction of Tomato Plant Disease by Using Machine Learning System
items.abstract: One of the most extensively grown and economically important vegetable crops in the world, tomatoes (Solanum Lycopersicon) are prized for both their commercial demand and nutritional worth. Despite its significance, a number of diseases brought on by bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens as well as adverse environmental factors negatively impact tomato cultivation. If these illnesses are not identified and treated early on, they may result in significant production and quality losses. Conventional disease detection techniques mostly rely on farmers' or specialists' manual visual inspection, which is time-consuming, labour-intensive, subjective, and frequently unfeasible for large-scale farming. Recent developments in image processing and machine learning have made automated plant disease detection systems dependable substitutes for prompt and precise diagnosis. Using a mixed machine learning architecture, this study suggests an intelligent tomato plant disease prediction system. The suggested method uses Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for feature extraction after employing picture preprocessing techniques to improve visual attributes. K-Means clustering is used to further organise the retrieved characteristics, and a Support Vector Machine (SVM) is used to classify diseases. The suggested hybrid model performs better than traditional machine learning methods in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix metrics, according to experimental study. The findings demonstrate the system's resilience, scalability, and affordability, which positions it as a viable option for early disease diagnosis and increased agricultural output.

items.title: Identifying Robust Predictors of Operational Fatigue in Emergency Medical Services Providers: A Machine Learning Approach
items.abstract: Fatigue in emergency medical services (EMS) providers is associated with impaired performance and safety risk, yet data-driven fatigue modeling in EMS remains limited. This study investigated the feasibility of predicting operational fatigue using multimodal wearable physiological, behavioral, and contextual data obtained from 11 EMS providers during a 5-day real-world field data collection. Features were extracted from 6-hour retrospective temporal windows preceding fatigue assessments and used to train Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost models. Logistic Regression achieved the best predictive performance (AUROC = 0.87), demonstrating reliable discrimination between high- and low-fatigue states. Feature importance analyses identified robust fatigue predictors across models, including time of day, cumulative work exposure, dispatched call volume, and slope-based pulse rate features. Findings suggest that operational fatigue in EMS reflects interacting circadian, workload-related, behavioral, and physiological processes and supports the feasibility of scalable wearable-based fatigue monitoring in safety-critical operational environments.

items.title: iLeapTutor: a RAG-enabled generative AI platform for standards-aligned university course authoring
items.abstract: Introduction Recent advances in Artificial intelligence (AI) and Generative AI (GenAI) have enabled more dynamic digital learning experiences. Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) leverage this capability to improve learning outcomes by offering structured and responsive support. This paper introduces iLeap Tutor , an intelligent learning platform that delivers consistent, structured, course-aligned learning materials that meet course requirements, such as Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) and National E-learning Center (NeLC) standards. Methods iLeap Tutor uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the tutor's uploaded course materials together with Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (Preview), with prompts that embed the CLO and NeLC requirements, and the tutor reviews and approves the generated course. The platform was evaluated as a single-course proof-of-concept using the Selected Topics in Computer Science course at Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University (IAU). The generated content was assessed using BERTScore, Self-BLEU, and latency measurements, and thirteen academic experts evaluated the generated course in terms of content accuracy, alignment with CLOs, structure, language quality, and platform usability. Results The evaluation achieved a BERTScore-F1 of 0.829 and a cross-run Self-BLEU result of 0.553 and a within-lesson Self-BLEU of 0.146, while the generation of 16 course topics averaged 219 s in latency. At least 92.3% of responses on every questionnaire item indicated agreement, and all of them would recommend the platform. Discussion The results indicate strong semantic alignment and output consistency across multiple runs and within-lesson content diversity.

items.title: Impact of Documentation Aids on the Inclusion of Salient Left-Ventricular Late Gadolinium Enhancement Characteristics in Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging Impressions
items.abstract: Abstract Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is a key diagnostic and prognostic biomarker in ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) and nonischemic cardiomyopathy (NICM). However, the completeness of LGE reporting in routine CMR impressions remains incompletely characterized. We aimed to evaluate the impact of large language model (LLM)-assisted reporting on the consistency of LGE pattern, distribution, and severity documentation in CMR impressions for ICM and NICM. We analyzed 828 unstructured (1990–2023) and 400 structured (2024–2025) CMR reports to identify documentation of LGE pattern, distribution, and severity. A Llama 3 language model fine-tuned on 27,000 structured CMR reports was used to generate 9650 CMR impressions; LGE attributes were extracted using an LLM judge. LLM reporting behavior was further assessed using quantized low-rank adaptation adapters trained on structured and unstructured impressions. Structured reporting captured LGE pattern more frequently than unstructured reporting overall (85.5% vs. 61.0%, p = 9.60 × 10 −7 ) and for ICM (90.0% vs. 69.4%, p = 0.005). LLM-generated impressions demonstrated more frequent reporting of LGE distribution (75.3%) and severity (70.9%) versus structured and unstructured reports ( p < 0.001). Fine-tuning with an adapter trained on unstructured impressions significantly improved reporting of all three LGE attributes. Structured reporting improved LGE pattern documentation, but gaps in LGE distribution and severity documentation persisted across human report formats. LLM-generated impressions achieved broader attribute coverage for LGE distribution and severity. Fine-tuning on unstructured data improved model performance, suggesting that passive augmentation with data capturing the documentation styles of multiple providers may help to address reporting gaps.

items.abstract: This paper presents a domain-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework that mitigates hallucinations and is designed to strengthen factual consistency in large language model (LLM)-based question-answering systems.Here, hallucination is operationally defined in this study as the generation of an unsupported substantive response to an unanswerable question.Existing RAG frameworks may produce less reliable responses due to retrieval failures or noisy retrieved content, potentially leading to inaccurate or unsupported answers.These limitations are especially problematic in domain-specific applications where factual accuracy is essential, and even minor errors can undermine user trust.To address these issues, this study proposes an enhanced RAG architecture that combines hierarchical metadata retrieval with fact-grounded prompt constraints.Hierarchical metadata retrieval narrows the search space in a structured manner, thereby reducing the amount of irrelevant or noisy information passed to the generation module.Fact-grounded prompt constraints further guide the LLM to generate responses grounded in the retrieved evidence.This study evaluated a Pure LLM, a Basic RAG model, and the proposed model using an internally constructed evaluation set of 210 questions, comprising 105 answerable questions and 105 synthetically generated unanswerable questions.Qwen2.5-14B was used for response generation, and the Ragas framework was used for performance evaluation.Compared with the Basic RAG baseline, the proposed model achieved a higher Faithfulness score (0.8926 vs. 0.7366) among the substantive responses generated by each model.These findings suggest that coordinated control of the retrieval and generation stages may improve abstention behavior and response grounding in the evaluated domain-specific RAG setting.However, the framework's generalizability to other domains requires further empirical validation.

items.title: INNOVATIVE APPROACHES IN MARKETING: PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT AND PROMOTION IN THE CONTEXT OF DIGITALIZATION
items.abstract: The modern approach to product creation is based not on intuitive ideas, but on the real-time analysis of users' digital behavior. It allows for predicting audience demands and actively shaping them by adapting the product to specific scenarios. Amid information overload, consumers place high demands on the quality and personalization of service. To build long-term relationships with the audience, brands need to ensure a seamless digital experience at all stages of interaction. The article explores modern innovative approaches to product development and promotion within the context of the economy's digital transformation. Special attention is paid to how digitalization is changing the logic of product creation and marketing communications: the focus shifts toward data, the speed of response to market demands, and the delivery of a seamless customer experience. The transformation of the product lifecycle stages is analyzed separately, covering the acceleration of time-to-market for new products through digital prototyping and split testing, dynamic positioning management based on real-time analytics, and the adaptation of promotion strategies to audience behavior on social media and marketplaces. The key tools shaping these new practices are examined, including artificial intelligence and machine learning for demand forecasting and offer adaptation, big data for segmentation and hypothesis testing, immersive technologies for audience engagement, and omnichannel systems. The research results allow for systemizing current innovative methods and offering practical recommendations for their implementation in organizations' marketing activities, taking into account the business's level of digital maturity and the specifics of the target audience. The recommendations on innovative approaches have been tested at an Omsk confectionery enterprise. The article will be of interest to corporate executives, marketers, and brand managers.

items.title: Innovative Non-Thermal and Advanced Processing Technologies for Optimizing Nutrient Retention and Extending Food Shelf Life: Integration of Machine Learning for Process Optimization
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: Conventional thermal processing methods such as drying, salting, fermentation, pasteurization, and sterilization remain the backbone of food processing and preservation. However, heat-induced losses of vitamins, pigments, bioactive compounds, and texture quality often compel manufacturers to explore alternative approaches to satisfy evolving consumer demands. In response to the increasing preference for minimally processed foods that retain nutritional quality and fresh-like characteristics, researchers and industry stakeholders have turned to innovative non-thermal and advanced processing technologies. This comprehensive review evaluates the current landscape of non-thermal technologies, including high hydrostatic pressure (HHP), pulsed electric field (PEF), ultrasonication (US), cold plasma (CP), UV irradiation (UVC), and ozonation, that effectively inactivate spoilage and pathogenic microorganisms while operating at ambient or modest temperatures. Additionally, recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) optimization for these technologies are explored, highlighting their potential to enhance process efficiency, predict microbial inactivation kinetics, and optimize nutritional retention. These methods preserve sensory qualities, improve techno-functional properties, support better digestibility and oxidative stability, and significantly extend shelf life across various food matrices with minimal thermal degradation. Keywords: Food processing, non-thermal technologies, hydrostatic pressure, ultrasonication, ozonation, oxidative stability, machine learning, artificial intelligence, process optimization

items.title: Inquiétudes et Attentes des Chirurgiens-Dentistes Ivoiriens sur l'Intégration de l'Intelligence Artificielle en Odontologie : Une Étude Descriptive Transversale
items.abstract: RÉSUMÉIntroduction. L'intelligence artificielle (IA) constitue une innovation majeure susceptible de transformer les pratiques dentaires, mais son intégration dans les pays en développement soulève des questions spécifiques. Cette étude avait pour but d'explorer les inquiétudes et les attentes des chirurgiens-dentistes ivoiriens concernant l'intégration de l'IA en odontologie. Méthodologie. Étude descriptive et transversale menée de janvier à mai 2025 à Abidjan, auprès de 68 chirurgiens-dentistes en exercice, volontaires et consentants. Les étudiants en formation initiale et les praticiens retraités ont été exclus. L'échantillonnage était stratifié proportionnel selon le type de structure d'exercice (public et privé), avec une sélection aléatoire simple au sein de chaque strate. Les données ont été recueillies par un questionnaire standardisé auto-administré, pré-testé auprès de 15 praticiens, structuré en cinq sections : données sociodémographiques, connaissances sur l'IA, perceptions générales, attentes et perspectives, et dispositions à adopter l'IA. Les données ont été saisies et analysées avec IBM SPSS Statistics version 25. Résultats. L'âge moyen des praticiens était de moins de 30 ans dans 41 % des cas, et 53 % avaient moins de 5 ans d'expérience. La grande majorité (96 %) avait déjà entendu parler de l'IA appliquée à l'odontologie, mais 84 % n'avaient jamais utilisé d'outils d'IA dans leur pratique. L'imagerie radiographique constituait le domaine le plus influencé (88 %). La majorité (94 %) considérait que l'IA pourrait améliorer la pratique odontologique. Les principales inquiétudes étaient la déshumanisation de la relation patient-praticien (62 %) et le coût élevé des équipements (59 %). Tous les participants se déclaraient favorables à une formation en IA, privilégiant les ateliers pratiques en présentiel (50–55 %). Conclusion. L'IA représente une opportunité importante pour le développement de l'odontologie en Côte d'Ivoire. Son intégration effective nécessite une meilleure formation des praticiens, une accessibilité accrue aux technologies et un encadrement éthique et réglementaire adapté.ABSTRACTIntroduction. Artificial intelligence (AI) is a major innovation likely to transform dental practices, but its integration in developing countries raises specific questions. This study had as its purpose to explore the concerns and expectations of Ivorian dentists regarding the integration of AI in dentistry. Methods. A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted from January to May 2025 in Abidjan, among 68 practising dentists who were volunteers and consented. Students in initial training and retired practitioners were excluded. Proportional stratified sampling by type of practice (public and private) was used, with simple random selection within each stratum. Data were collected using a standardized self-administered questionnaire, pre-tested with 15 practitioners, structured in five sections: sociodemographic data, knowledge about AI, general perceptions, expectations and perspectives, and willingness to adopt AI. Data were entered and analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 25. Results. The age group under 30 years was the most represented (41%), and 53% had less than 5 years of experience. The vast majority (96%) had heard of AI applied to dentistry, but 84% had never used AI-based tools in their practice. Radiographic imaging was the area most influenced (88%). Most practitioners (94%) believed that AI could improve dental practice. The main concerns were dehumanization of the patient-practitioner relationship (62%) and the high cost of equipment (59%). All participants were in favour of AI training, preferring practical in-person workshops (50–55%). Conclusion. AI represents a significant opportunity for the development of dentistry in Côte d'Ivoire. Its effective integration requires better training for practitioners, increased access to technology, and appropriate ethical and regulatory oversight.

items.title: Inspection-aware industrial augmented reality: integrated concepts and preliminary validation for extending an AR-AI station for component recovery from washing machines
items.abstract: This study presents an extension of an industrial augmented reality (AR) and artificial intelligence (AI) disassembly station with inspection functions for reusable components recovered from end-of-life washing machines. While prior work focused on monitor-based AR guidance and AI-supported validation of disassembly steps, this paper addresses the next integration step: inspection-aware AR workflows that connect worker guidance, AI/sensor-based condition assessment, human confirmation, and reuse documentation. Specifically, we outline how inspection procedures for the two most valuable components targeted for reuse (printed circuit boards (PCBs) and the washing unit) can be integrated into the station concept. For PCBs, a burn-damage classification pipeline was developed. Preliminary frame-level validation on an independent real-world dataset showed that several models detect most visibly burnt PCB views, but their low specificity currently prevents autonomous reuse decisions. The AI component is therefore used as a preliminary screening and warning mechanism whose output is reviewed by the worker. For the washing unit, the developed testing device demonstrates the feasibility of pressure-loss and vibration measurements directly after disassembly; these measurements are presently proof-of-concept demonstrations rather than quantitatively validated diagnostics. The primary contribution of this Brief Research Report is therefore the system-level integration of AR guidance, visual and sensor-based assessment, human confirmation, reuse classification, and documentation into one continuous worker-facing workflow. The results establish integrated feasibility and preliminary validation rather than industrial inspection reliability.

items.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chatbots to Promote Health Behaviors in Adolescents
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Adolescence is a critical developmental period for establishing health behaviors that shape long-term well-being and chronic disease risk. However, many adolescents do not meet recommendations for physical activity (PA), diet, screen time, or sleep. This review examines the use of AI chatbots to promote adolescents’ health behaviors. It synthesizes the existing literature on the use of AI chatbots to promote adolescents’ health behaviors, with a focus on four areas: design, feasibility, impact, safety and ethics. Methods: This narrative review synthesized adolescent-focused studies and relevant studies involving children, young adults, mixed-age samples, or unspecified populations when their findings were applicable to adolescent health behavior interventions. The evidence was organized around chatbot design, feasibility, behavioral outcomes, and safety and ethical issues. Results: Selected studies reported favorable usability, satisfaction, or engagement during brief evaluations. Adaptive personalization, contextual prompting, and theory-guided dialogue were reported design features, but their contributions to sustained engagement or behavioral outcomes remain uncertain. However, evidence of behavioral impact of AI chatbots remains limited and uneven across behavior domains (i.e., PA, dietary intake, screen time, and sleep). Safety and ethical concerns include accuracy and misinformation, privacy and data governance, and clear escalation and safety protocols. Conclusions: AI chatbots warrant further investigation for adolescent health behavior promotion. Current evidence does not establish general acceptability, sustained engagement, or behavior change efficacy, and further research should evaluate these outcomes alongside safety and ethical safeguards.

items.title: Integrating generative AI and reference management tools in assignment writing: insights from an ODeL context
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and reference management technologies is transforming academic writing practices in higher education. This qualitative instrumental case study investigates how generative AI and reference management tools are integrated into assignment writing at Zimbabwe Open University within an Open and Distance eLearning (ODeL) environment. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with seven lecturers and one quality assurance coordinator, as well as focus group discussions with fourteen students selected through purposive sampling. Guided by the Constructivist Learning Theory, the study examined the pedagogical implications of AI-supported writing practices. Findings reveal that tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly and Mendeley enhance writing quality, research efficiency, accessibility, and learner confidence. However, concerns regarding overreliance, academic integrity and diminished critical engagement were also identified. The study recommends the development of institutional policies, ethical training frameworks and curriculum adjustments to promote responsible and pedagogically sound integration of generative AI tools in ODeL contexts.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial en ecocardiografía canina: revisión narrativa de métodos, validación y retos técnicos
items.abstract: Objective: This review critically examined artificial intelligence (AI) applications in canine echocardiography, automated measurement and disease classification strategies, validation designs, and the requirements for safe clinical translation. Method: A narrative review was conducted. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched on 20 October 2026, supplemented by screening the reference lists of identified articles, and studies that applied machine learning or deep learning to canine echocardiograms were selected by relevance. Results: In the clinical veterinary setting, two studies addressed automated ventricular measurements through anatomical landmark localization and staging of myxomatous mitral valve disease through echocardiography–radiography fusion. An additional group of experimental studies applied deep learning to left ventricular segmentation and motion tracking in dogs. The main challenges identified were operator variability, breed-related anatomical heterogeneity, the lack of multicenter validation, and reliance on imperfect reference standards. Conclusions: The clinical usefulness of these models requires patient- and center-level evaluation, uncertainty quantification, agreement studies against specialists, and analysis of errors near treatment thresholds. A two-stage research pathway, measurement followed by classification, was proposed, complemented by prospective assessment and veterinary oversight.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial generativa y escritura autorregulada
items.abstract: In the context of foreign language writing, studies suggest that Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)-assisted learning supports knowledge acquisition and increases motivation (Chen & Gong, 2025). However, its use requires a meticulous implementation due to deficiencies in academic rigor and citation accuracy, as well as the risk of over-reliance (Chen & Gong, 2025; Solak, 2024). Through a quasi-experimental design with pre- and post-intervention measures, this study evaluates the efficacy of a GenAI-mediated pedagogical sequence on argumentative writing performance. Following a process-based writing approach (Flower & Hayes, 1981), 39 second-year English Language Teaching (ELT) students participated in five sessions focused on self-assessment and draft editing. These sessions were assisted by tools such as Gemin (for IELTS rubric-based draft evaluation), Quillbot (for grammar and style correction), and Lextutor (for lexical profiling). The results confirm that GenAI —when integrated into a structured sequence— seems to strengthen L2 writing clarity, making it more precise and readable by optimizing feedback and promoting the critical, self-regulated use of these tools for essay improvement. Furthermore, the high level of student satisfaction with the resources used highlights the importance of fostering digital literacy and enhancing the role of GenAI as a pedagogical complement. This approach promotes the ethical integration of emerging technologies into writing instruction within Higher Education.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial y competencias de aprendizaje en programación
items.abstract: The expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education programming raises questions about its influence on learning autonomy and critical thinking. This stems from theoretical concerns about technological dependency and from the limited regional empirical evidence on how these effects vary by experience level. This quantitative study examines whether experience level (novices vs. advanced) and AI usage frequency associate with these constructs among computer science students in Costa Rica. Using a cross-sectional design, 99 students from Universidad Hispanoamericana de Costa Rica were classified as novices (n = 79) or advanced (n = 20), via the Dreyfus & Dreyfus (1986) model with 5 weighted indicators. Accordingly, autonomy (а = 0,685) and critical thinking (а = 0,742) were measured, and both constructs were analyzed using Welch t-tests, Pearson correlations, and multiple regression. Autonomy showed suggestive evidence of being higher in advanced students [t(49,2) = 2,079, p = 0,043, g = 0,386], though nonparametric analysis did not confirm this [U = 614,5, p = 0,125]. Critical thinking showed no significant difference [t(42,1) = 1,816, p = 0,077, g = 0,361], and AI usage frequency was not associated with autonomy [r = 0,166, p = 0,101] or critical thinking [r = 0,123, p = 0,226]. Both constructs showed robust correlation [r = 0,552, p < 0,001; р = 0,533, p < 0,001]. The 88,9 % active modification rate suggests students use AI as cognitive support, potentially explaining the null associations. Given that 85,9 % support regulated use and 10,1 % favor prohibition, these preliminary findings suggest that promoting ethical regulated AI use may be preferable to restriction.

items.title: Intelligent Assistive Technologies in Higher Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education by enabling intelligent assistive technologies that enhance learning outcomes for students with disabilities. This chapter examines the landscape of AI-driven assistive tools—including speech recognition, adaptive learning platforms, natural language processing, and predictive analytics—and their role in advancing inclusive education. Drawing on recent systematic reviews and empirical studies, it critically evaluates opportunities such as personalized accommodation, improved accessibility, and universal design for learning (UDL) integration, alongside challenges including algorithmic bias, data privacy, and digital equity. Frameworks for ethical AI deployment and institutional policy recommendations are presented. The chapter concludes with future directions for sustainable, human-centered AI assistive ecosystems in higher education.

items.title: Intelligent Financial Forecasting Using Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Techniques
items.abstract: Financial forecasting is a core aspect of contemporary financial systems, and it helps to support some of the most important activities of a financial system, including investment planning, portfolio optimization, and risk management. The traditional forecasting models, which are mainly statistical and econometric models, are often based on assumptions of linearity and limited datasets and therefore have limited capability to accurately model the complex, volatile and nonlinear behaviour of financial markets. This paper will give a detailed comparison and contrast of the different AI and ML methods used in financial forecasting, such support vectors machines (SVM), artificial neural networks (ANN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, reinforcement learning (RL) and natural language processing (NLP). Overall, this paper demonstrates that AI and ML can have a transformative potential in the context of financial forecasting because it has the potential to develop more intelligent, responsive and efficient financial decision-making systems.

items.title: Introduction
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has disrupted established assessment practices in higher education, producing widespread uncertainty about what counts as appropriate student work and how it should be evaluated. The introductory chapter argues that this uncertainty is not simply a temporary lack of clarity but reflects a deeper challenge in how assessment distinguishes between student achievement and the tools students use. Drawing on the idea of wicked problems, it suggests that this challenge cannot be definitively resolved, but must instead be worked through in context by focusing on how boundaries in assessment are being drawn, interpreted, and contested under AI conditions. This introduction uses this framing to orient the chapters that follow, showing how they contribute to understanding and respond to these changes from different perspectives. The volume that follows then brings together conceptual, empirical, and forward-looking work to examine how assessment is evolving, why these changes matter, and how educators might respond. Rather than offering a single model of AI-ready assessment, it provides a set of resources for understanding the problem and navigating it in practice.

items.title: Introduction
items.abstract: This introduction sets out the problem the book addresses: the absence of a comprehensive framework under African human rights law governing the use of artificial intelligence by social media platforms. It situates that problem within the rapid global adoption of artificial intelligence across public and private sectors, the proliferation of national and regional strategies and ethical principles, and the African vision on the regulation of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. It explains why social media platforms occupy a central place in this debate, given business models built on retention and the suitability of artificial intelligence for inference, personalisation, and targeting at scale. The introduction then sets out the book’s structure, explaining the selection of three rights most affected by these technologies, and the rationale for treating each according to the developmental stage of the right within African jurisprudence.

items.title: Introduction to AI-Driven Multimodal Systems
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence is pushing beyond unimodal paradigms, paving the way for sophisticated multimodal systems that can process and relate information from diverse sources such as text, images, audio, and sensor data. This chapter serves as a foundational introduction to AI-driven multimodal intelligence, outlining the core principles, architectures, and transformative potential of these systems. We begin by defining key concepts, contrasting multimodal learning with traditional unimodal approaches, and highlighting the inherent challenges of data heterogeneity, alignment, and fusion. The chapter then delves into the primary technical architectures for multimodal integration, including early, late, and hybrid fusion strategies, with a focus on modern neural approaches like cross-modal attention and transformers. Beyond the algorithms, we discuss the critical pipeline from data processing and feature extraction to model training and cross-modal reasoning. Finally, the chapter sets the stage for the rest of the book by underscoring the real-world implications of this technology, from enhancing accessibility to revolutionizing human–computer interaction, while also acknowledging the ongoing research challenges in robustness, interpretability, and ethical deployment.

items.title: Investigating ChatGPT’s Impact on Developing the Tertiary-Level English Department Students’ EFL Writing Skills
items.abstract: Despite the growing body of research involving examining teachers’ and students’ experiences of AI integration in EFL writing pedagogy in Bangladesh, relatively little is known about English department students’ perceptions of ChatGPT’s influence in major domains of EFL writing. To bridge this gap, our research investigates tertiary-level English department students’ perceptions of ChatGPT’s impact in developing their EFL writing skills within the Bangladeshi context through employing a mixed-method research design, comprising both quantitative and qualitative data. Quantitative data were collected from 74 undergraduate and graduate students at a public university in Bangladesh using a structured five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and subsequently, qualitative insights were gathered to supplement the survey data through three focus group discussions (FGDs). Our study explored ChatGPT’s perceived role across four key domains of EFL writing: motivation and engagement, grammatical correction, writing essays and creating references. Findings revealed that ChatGPT positively influenced students’ motivation through providing immediate and non-judgmental feedback, facilitating idea generation, content organization and context-specific writing. Also, ChatGPT facilitated the pre-writing and foundational stages of essay writing. Students exhibited more caution regarding ChatGPT’s role as a grammar correction and referencing tool. Despite its usefulness in explaining grammar rules and providing language-related feedback, students found specialized grammar correction tools to be more reliable than ChatGPT. Likewise, ChatGPT emerged as an unreliable referencing tool due to producing misleading citation information. Our study offers key implications for educators, stakeholders and policy- makers to integrate ChatGPT more ethically and effectively in EFL writing while preserving independent reasoning and judicious evaluation. items.title: Investigating the Effect of User Onboarding and Task Demonstration on Training Performance and Learning in a Multiuser AR Learning Environment
items.abstract: Collaborative augmented reality (AR) systems are increasingly used for technical training, yet limited evidence exists on how instructional design choices affect learning and transfer. This study examined the effects of onboarding strategy and task demonstration modality in a multiuser AR environment for motor control unit setup and lockout-tagout training. Eighty participants were assigned to one of four conditions in a 2 × 2 between-subjects study: checklist versus interactive onboarding and video versus avatar-based demonstration. Participants completed AR-based training and then performed the procedure on physical equipment. Results showed that avatar-based demonstrations produced significantly greater learning gains, while video-based demonstrations produced fewer procedural errors during physical transfer. Onboarding strategy did not significantly affect objective learning or transfer outcomes. These findings reveal an important design tradeoff: immersive avatar demonstrations may strengthen conceptual understanding, whereas physically grounded video demonstrations may better support real-world procedural transfer. The study provides evidence-based guidance for designing collaborative AR training systems in technical workforce education.

items.title: Investigating the Efficacy of the Gemini 2.5 Pro Model in the Estimation of Macronutrient Content
items.abstract: Health guidance is a topic that has been gaining increasing traction in the past few years. Specifically, apps utilizing AI to provide health guidance and allow users to track macronutrient content have been gaining prevalence in recent research. However, current apps require users to manually input all information into the app. Therefore, this work seeks to evaluate the effectiveness of the Gemini 2.5 Pro model, a multimodal large language model (LLM), in analyzing the macronutrient content (i.e., proteins, fats, and carbohydrates) in food images. We tested 100 dishes randomly sampled from the Nutrition5k dataset. Each image was queried three times with three different prompt phrasings and the estimated values were compared with the ground truth values in the dataset. For the baseline prompt, the mean absolute error (MAE) was 4.1 g for protein, 3.6 g for fat, and 6.1 g for carbohydrates, and the median absolute percentage errors were 29.9%, 29.2%, and 32.1% respectively. The mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) was 38.5% for protein but 211.2% for fats and 442.7% for carbohydrates, which were inflated due to a small number of dishes containing less than 0.5 g of fat or carbohydrate, where errors of a few grams produced errors in the thousands. Without dishes with less than 2 g of the nutrient, the MAPE was 38.5%, 33.6%, and 33.5%. On metrics not sensitive to near-zero values, error was of similar size across the three macronutrients, and protein was underestimated on average, with the largest errors concentrated in a subset of dishes. MAE differed by at most 0.6 g across prompt wordings, although fat MdAPE was higher under both alternative prompts. Because no confidence intervals or significance tests were computed, these are observations from a single 100-dish sample rather than established differences. Additionally, the 100 dishes selected for the study came from a 400-dish subset whose selection cannot be reproduced.

items.title: Investigating the Utility of LLM-Based “Silicon Samples” in Political Science Conjoint Experiments
items.abstract: Abstract This research note is the first study to explore the viability of using LLM-generated respondents in forced-choice conjoint experiments. I generate naive “silicon samples” using three models, GPT 4o-Mini, Llama 3.2, and Magistral-small-2506, benchmarked to a large sample of live conjoint respondents, allowing for direct comparisons between human and silicon choices. The resulting analyses suggest that naively generated silicon samples are insufficient to simulate human decision-making in conjoint tasks; these results also suggest that there are systemic differences in the way demographic covariates shape LLM and human choices in experimental contexts. In total, this analysis makes two important contributions: it establishes a descriptive baseline understanding of LLM-generated respondent performance in conjoint experiments and suggests that naive silicon samples cannot accurately infer human choices using demographic traits in experimental decision making contexts. Finally, the implications of these results imply that LLMs consider covariates differently than live respondents do in micro-level decision making contexts.

items.abstract: This chapter examines the principles and structures that underpin effective investigation management, and it emphasises that organised processes, robust governance, and strategic oversight enhance investigative success and safeguard justice. It outlines governance frameworks, clarifies the role of the (P)GSB, and establishes an Overarching Investigative Strategy that integrates major incident rooms, allocates appropriate resources, and defines enquiry team roles. Finally, the chapter addresses disclosure obligations and demonstrates that disciplined management, transparent processes, and continuous evaluation ensure accountability, reduce error, and maintain investigative integrity.

items.title: Is Gen AI an editor or a revision tool? A case study of EFL students in AI-assisted revision
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) tools become increasingly integrated into language education, understanding how learners respond to AI-generated feedback during writing revision has become an important research concern. Existing studies have primarily examined the effects of AI on writing performance, with less attention to learners’ reported decision-making and reflection during revision. This qualitative study investigated learner-AI interaction, reported revision practices and learner perceptions among 18 first-year non-English-major students enrolled in a university EFL writing course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews following a Gen AI-assisted revision task and analysed using thematic analysis. The findings identified three interaction patterns with Gen AI: passive AI reliance, adaptive AI engagement, metacognitive AI engagement. Participants differed in how they evaluated and used AI-generated feedback, including passive acceptance, selective uptake, and critical evaluation. Some reported increased confidence, motivation, and awareness of linguistic form, whereas others expressed concerns about overreliance, authorship, and loss of personal voice. These self-reported experiences provide insight into how EFL learners perceive and manage GenAI-assisted revision, highlighting the need for pedagogical approaches that foster critical AI literacy and reflective learner autonomy.

items.title: It’s Not the Tool, It’s the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems can now reliably solve many standard tasks used in introductory physics courses, producing correct equations, graphs, and explanations. While this capability is often framed as an opportunity for efficiency or personalization, it also poses a subtle ethical and educational risk: students may increasingly submit correct results without engaging in the epistemic practices that define learning physics. This challenge has recently been described as the "boiling frog problem" because we may not fully recognize how rapidly AI capabilities are advancing and fail to respond with commensurate urgency. In this article, we argue that the central challenge of AI in physics education is not cheating or tool selection, but instructional design. Drawing on research on self-regulated learning, cognitive load, multiple representations, and hybrid intelligence, we propose a practical framework for cognitively activated learning activities that structures student activities before, during, and after AI use. Using an example from an introductory kinematics laboratory, we show how AI can be integrated in ways that preserve prediction, interpretation, and evaluation as core learning activities. Rather than treating AI as an answer-generating tool, the framework positions AI as an epistemic partner whose contributions are deliberately bounded and reflected upon.

items.title: Knowledge Acquisition Methods and Conceptual Mastery Outcomes in Private Institutions of Learning in Uganda
items.abstract: For one to achieve meaningful learning, Knowledge acquisition is a very crucial factor that should never be undermined, however, we should also note that the learner's possession of information does not necessarily mean that he understands all the concepts or is able to apply them in unfamiliar situations. This narrative literature review examines how knowledge acquisition methods may shape conceptual mastery in private institutions of learning in Uganda. It examines and brings together the conceptual and theoretical perspectives represented in the literature cited by different authors, including constructivist learning, deep approaches to learning, critical thinking, collaborative learning, inquiry-based learning, experiential learning, formative assessment, and technology-supported instruction. The review also looks at the advantages and disadvantages of artificial intelligence and digital knowledge-management tools. The reviewed literature consistently argues that conceptual mastery occurs when learners actively connect new material with prior knowledge, explain ideas, investigate problems, receive feedback, reflect on their learning, and transfer knowledge to authentic tasks. Lectures and other educators can provide all the necessary explanations and provide foundational knowledge, but they may not support mastery when they are used as the only instructional method or when majorly paired with recall-based examinations. items.title: LaplaceReason: A Certified Benchmark and Continuous Dynamic Systems Reasoning Suite for Frontier Large Language Models
items.abstract: Abstract: Frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) such as DeepSeek-R1, OpenAI o1/o3, and Qwen-2.5-Math have achieved near-human proficiency on discrete reasoning benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH). However, they systematically exhibit catastrophic hallucination, severe phase lag, and structural divergence when evaluated on continuous dynamic systems, multiscale stiff ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and high-order operational calculus. Traditional synthetic data pipelines fail to provide reliable supervision for these domains because conventional computer algebra solvers suffer from Wilkinson's catastrophic conditioning when factorizing high-order characteristic polynomials (K > 18). In this work, we present LaplaceReason, the first certified, massive reasoning benchmark designed to evaluate and train frontier LLMs on continuous multi-physics and dynamic systems. Ground truth solutions and step-by-step reasoning trajectories are certified via a deterministic, high-precision operational oracle guaranteeing machine-precision residual bounds (||R||_inf < 10^-14) across arbitrary orders without numerical root-finding. The benchmark spans seven fundamental task families:1. High-order rational dynamics (K from 2 to 60)2. Multiscale stiff ODEs (stiffness ratio S > 100x)3. Real-time randomized SVD with universal Gavish-Donoho noise rank thresholding4. 3D tomographic C-scan reconstruction5. Sub-millisecond zero-lag kinematic trajectory extrapolation6. Matrix-pencil modal extraction without Fourier spectral leakage7. items.title: Large language models as enablers of industrial information integration in construction: an adoption mechanism study
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are emerging enablers of industrial information integration, yet their adoption mechanisms in construction remain unclear. This study develops an integrated framework that combines the Technology Acceptance Model and the Information Systems Success model, extended with trust, prior LLM experience, perceived substitution crisis, and job specialization, to explain individual adoption of LLMs for information integration in construction. Data from a cross-sectional survey of 82 Chinese construction professionals are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and bootstrapping. Results show that perceived ease of use robustly strengthens attitude and provides directional evidence for strengthening perceived usefulness, while perceived usefulness strengthens attitude and attitude drives intention to use. Trust, reinforced by perceived information quality, shows a positive association with intention under the primary one-tailed criterion, but this relationship requires further validation under the two-tailed robustness check. System quality and information quality indirectly foster adoption by improving perceived ease of use, although the relationship between system quality and trust is supported only as directional evidence, while prior LLM experience enhances ease of use but not perceived usefulness or trust. Perceived substitution crisis and job specialization exhibit no significant effects. The findings highlight that successful LLM-enabled information integration depends on both technical quality and psychological appraisals, and they offer implications for designing trustworthy, humancentered LLM applications that advance intelligent, interconnected construction ecosystems. The study links micro-level user acceptance with macro-level digital transformation and integration strategic objectives.

items.title: Leading Equity-Focused School and District Improvement With GenAI: The Human-AI Team Improvement Framework
items.abstract: This theoretical paper examines how educational leaders can leverage generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for equity-focused school and district improvement. Although prior improvement leadership research connects equity-focused leadership, improvement science, and workplace culture (Shepard, 2026), AI use in education remains largely focused on individual use, leaving less understood about what changes when GenAI becomes part of an improvement team. Drawing on equity-focused leadership, improvement science, workplace culture, and human-AI teaming, the paper introduces the Human-AI Team Improvement Framework. The framework centers equity-focused collaborative continuous improvement and identifies three interdependent leadership conditions (co-inquiry, empowered ownership, and courageous safety) that support humans and GenAI in working, learning, and improving together. The framework focuses attention on the leadership conditions needed for human-AI teams to work and learn together in improvement. It suggests that GenAI may help teams address immediate problems while also building their capacity to inquire, learn, and improve. The paper concludes with implications for educational leaders and directions for research on human-AI improvement teams in practice.

items.title: Leading the Redesign: Purpose, Ecosystems and Sequencing in School Leadership for AI
items.abstract: Most school responses to generative AI begin with tools: which platform to license, which training day to run, which policy to publish. This article argues that the order is backwards. Drawing on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside research on curriculum reform and institutional change, it examines AI in schools as a leadership problem. It sets out five pressures that leaders face: a speed gap between students' adoption of AI and institutions' capacity to govern it; a purpose question about what school is for when knowledge is freely available; an ecosystem problem, in which reforms fail not at the design stage but in the system of assessment, professional learning and routines they land in; a sequencing problem, in which institutions buy tools before doing the human work that makes them useful; and a structural shift in which families increasingly unbundle schooling. It proposes a five-step leadership sequence (purpose, conversation, red lines, ecosystem align‐ ment and iteration) and argues that leaders should separate two decisions that are usually treated as one: what AI should free time for, and how fast the institution should move.

items.title: Learn First, Then Use AI: Testing an Expert Consensus on Generative AI and Learning Against the Empirical Evidence
items.abstract: Debate about generative AI in education often asks whether it is good or bad for learning. A 2026 expert consensus report from the University of Minnesota, UNC-Chapel Hill and UC Irvine argues that this question is too blunt. Thirty experts used a preregistered Delphi method to rate 65 learning processes for how likely general-purpose generative AI is to enhance or disrupt them, reaching consensus on 42. The pattern they describe can be read as a sequence: AI threatens the early work of taking in new information, can support the consolidation of what has been learned, and does not yet reliably support higher-order thinking and transfer. The report also rates the strength of the existing evidence as low. This review asks whether the experimental and observational studies published so far are consistent with that consensus. It maps a field experiment with high-school mathematics students, a randomised con‐ trolled trial of an AI physics tutor, an EEG study of essay writing, and survey research on cognitive offloading onto the three stages of the sequence. The studies largely agree with the experts. Unrestricted answer-giving harms acquisition. Tutor-style designs built on learning science can strengthen consolidation. Offloading thinking is linked with weaker critical thinking. We summarise this as a 'learn first, then use AI' principle, link it to established learning science, and set out implications for teachers, school leaders and researchers.

items.title: Learning designers and assessment practice in the age of AI
items.abstract: This chapter examines how learning designers (LDs) mediate and lead assessment transformation in higher education in response to the rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Drawing on cross-institutional interviews with 11 LDs from six Australian and New Zealand universities, it identifies ways that LDs are enacting their roles in response to GenAI: agents of change; emotional and cultural navigators; strategic influencers and policy shapers; designers of assessment; technical specialists and tool curators; and advocates for equity and inclusion. Situated within Whitchurch’s notion of the third space , LDs act as boundary spanners who translate institutional imperatives and academic values into coherent pedagogical practice. Their work supports transforming institutional ‘AI shock’ into opportunities for innovation, embedding authentic, reflective, and inclusive assessment practices. The chapter argues that LDs’ relational and strategic expertise is valuable in reimagining assessment for an AI-mediated educational future and calls for their recognition as co-leaders in shaping policy, pedagogy, and institutional culture.

items.title: Learning Processes in Science Teams: How Do Human-AI Scientists Learn From Each Other While Developing Collaborative AI
items.abstract: This study examines how scientists in interdisciplinary programs learn from one another during collaboration. Researchers who participated in large scale research projects on human-AI teaming were surveyed about their collaborative experiences. Survey results show that regular cross-team meetings, careful listening, and adaptive communication are central to effective integration, while terminology conflicts and coordination costs persist. Findings highlight interaction structures and integrative roles as key levers for improving interdisciplinary teamwork. Framed within the context of the science of team science, the discussion highlights the support needed for interdisciplinary structures and processes enabling effective scientific collaboration.

items.title: Legal Safeguards for Ai-Assisted Judicial Decision-Making: A Comparative Framework of Transparency, Human Oversight and Effective Remedies
items.abstract: Abstract Courts are adopting artificial intelligence faster than lawmakers are writing rules for it. Risk scores inform bail and sentencing, language models draft summaries and sometimes reasoning, and judicial councils issue guidance in the absence of statutes. This article asks what a litigant is legally entitled to when an AI system touches the decision that affects them. Using a doctrinal and functional comparative method, we examine binding and soft-law instruments from the European Union, the Council of Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, Brazil, Colombia and India, checked against official or reliable sources as of 26 October 2026. Three findings emerge. First, transparency duties are mostly addressed to institutions and regulators; the person whose liberty or rights are at stake rarely gets a right to know that AI was used, still less how. Second, human oversight is declared everywhere but engineered almost nowhere, despite strong evidence that nominal review produces automation bias rather than control. Third, remedies are the weakest link: with few exceptions, no instrument attaches a legal consequence to undisclosed or uncritical reliance on AI. We propose a Disclosure–Oversight–Remedy (DOR) framework that scales safeguards to the way AI is used, from auxiliary support to evaluative input, and prohibits determinative use. The framework converts principles into enforceable procedural entitlements and offers a template for legislators, judicial councils and courts.

items.title: Leveraging artificial intelligence for autonomous space healthcare: current evidence, operational architecture and research priorities for deep-space exploration
items.abstract: Introduction Deep-space missions will progressively limit real-time ground support, rapid evacuation and resupply, creating a need for medical capabilities that can operate with graded autonomy. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support this transition, but terrestrial performance cannot be equated with spaceflight readiness. Methods We conducted a narrative, hypothesis-generating review of literature relevant to AI-enabled space healthcare. Sources were selected iteratively for their contribution to health monitoring, biofluid analysis, medical imaging, clinical decision support or radiation assessment. The review did not use a systematic screening protocol or formal meta-analytic quality assessment; therefore, findings are synthesised qualitatively and claims are calibrated to evidence maturity. Results Evidence was grouped as spaceflight operational use, space-relevant prototype or analogue demonstration, terrestrial clinical validation, terrestrial experimental demonstration, or conceptual transfer. AI may support personalised monitoring, biofluid interpretation, ultrasound acquisition and analysis, radiation forecasting and clinical decision support. However, most cited applications remain terrestrial demonstrations. Key barriers include limited astronaut data, shifted physiological baselines, restricted computation and power, sensor and storage constraints, model drift, explainability, uncertainty management and failure handling. Conclusion AI is most plausibly deployed as one component of an integrated autonomous medical system that combines wearables and biosensors, onboard records, imaging, radiation monitoring, clinical decision support, crew oversight and delayed telemedical consultation. Near-term priorities are prospective validation in mission-relevant analogues, personalised baselines, resource-aware edge deployment, explicit uncertainty thresholds, human override and pre-defined safe fallback procedures. AI should augment rather than replace telemedicine and professional judgement.

items.title: Leveraging generative AI for human understanding: meta-requirements and design principles for Explanatory AI as an emerging paradigm
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support decision-making across critical domains, yet explainable AI (XAI) approaches prioritise algorithmic transparency over human comprehension. While XAI reveals computational processes for model validation, end users require explanations integrating domain knowledge, contextual reasoning, and professional frameworks. This disconnect reveals a design challenge: existing approaches fail to address how practitioners need to understand and act upon AI recommendations. This paper introduces Explanatory AI as an emerging complementary paradigm where AI systems leverage generative and multimodal capabilities to serve as explanatory partners for human understanding. Unlike traditional XAI, which answers ‘How did the algorithm decide?’ for validation purposes, Explanatory AI addresses ‘Why does this make sense?’ for practitioners making informed decisions. Through theory-informed design, we synthesise multidisciplinary perspectives from cognitive science, communication research, and education with empirical evidence from healthcare and AI expert interviews. Our analysis identifies five dimensions distinguishing Explanatory AI from XAI: explanatory purpose, communication mode, epistemic stance, adaptivity, and cognitive design. We derive five meta-requirements and formulate ten design principles prescribing how to build such systems, illustrated through five UI mockups exemplifying implementation. Explanatory AI operates standalone or combined with XAI, serving distinct purposes in creating systems that genuinely support human reasoning and decision-making.

items.title: Leveraging Mamba for Enhanced Multimodal Few-Shot Action Recognition
items.abstract: Few-Shot Action Recognition (FSAR) widely use in Action Recognition domains with limited labeled data, such as medical surgery. Existing FSAR methods often rely on single-modal approaches, which suffer from limited feature representation and a lack of semantic understanding. To overcome these limitations, we propose MoMA, a novel Mamba-based multimodal FSAR framework, designed to optimize the learning of multimodal information and improve the performance of few-shot action recognition tasks. MoMA integrates a multimodal large language model (MLLM) to generate semantically rich representations from both textual and video data, which are then aligned and fused with visual features. To address the challenges of domain-specific prior knowledge and intra-class variance, we introduce a dual-branch contrastive learning architecture that reinforces category distinctions and mitigates the accumulation of intra-class heterogeneity. Our experimental results show that MoMA outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the HMDB51, Kinetics, and SSv2 datasets, achieving improvements of 1.5%, 1.9%, and 3.5%, respectively, in the 1-shot setting.
